And a social worker who has worked extensively with him said he draws self-portraits that often show him with a tear running down his cheek. A self-portrait drawn by sniper Lee Boyd Malvo. According to social worker Carmeta Albarus-Lindo, Malvo is a changed person since he and John Allen Muhammad terrorized the Washington area five years ago this month in attacks that left 10 dead over a 23-day period. "The most I can do is to continue to be there, because that is his greatest fear -- that, you know, another parental figure would abandon him because that was what he'd been exposed to all his life," said Albarus-Lindo, who has spent hundreds of hours with Malvo since his arrest and conviction.  Read the letter » . She said one of those "parental" figures was Muhammad, who met Malvo in the Caribbean nearly two years before the deadly shooting spree began in 2002. Muhammad became the teenager's surrogate father, convincing him that violence was the only way to correct perceived injustices to African-Americans, Albarus-Lindo said. He ordered Malvo to go to bed each night and to memorize passages from "The Art of War," an ancient Chinese text on battlefield strategy. According to Albarus-Lindo, Malvo was "brainwashed" into aiding Muhammad in the murders. However, prosecutors have said Malvo, even at 17, knew what he was doing. "I thought he was coldblooded," said Paul Ebert, commonwealth attorney for Prince William County, Virginia, of the first time he met Malvo. "He was a person who had chosen a life of crime." And when a Virginia jury spared Malvo's life, some investigators said they were horrified. "That was the hardest day of my career," said April Carroll of the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms and Tobacco. "I felt that day we had failed when Malvo was not sentenced to death." Some of the victims' families said they are content that Malvo did not receive the death penalty. Vicki Buchanan Snyder, whose brother James "Sonny" Buchanan was shot in the back while mowing a patch of lawn at a Maryland auto dealership, said she was "satisfied" with the jury's verdict. As for Malvo, Albarus-Lindo said he will "never forgive himself for what has happened." When she first began seeing him, he still called Muhammad "Dad." It took months, she said, before he stopped. In the interim, Albarus-Lindo said, he took college correspondence courses and began to draw. Muhammad is at a Virginia prison called Sussex One. In a DVD made last year inside prison and obtained exclusively by CNN, he said he is "still fighting" on death row. He wants to "correct," he said, some "inaccurate statements" made by the news media about his relationship with Malvo. He wasn't specific about what he meant.  Watch Muhammad on death row » . Muhammad's ex-wife, Mildred, said she believed that she was the real target of the snipers from the beginning. She and her children live in suburban Washington, and she runs a Web site called Afterthetrauma.org, devoted to the victims of domestic abuse. Mildred Muhammad said she feels her ex-husband wanted to kill her as revenge because she was able to gain custody of their three children. As for his relationship with Malvo, she said she too is convinced that John Allen Muhammad brainwashed the younger man. "That boy was a victim before he even knew it," she said. "His life was over when he said, 'Hi.' " E-mail to a friend .

# The Sniper's Remorse: Reexamining Lee Boyd Malvo's Culpability

Lee Boyd Malvo, now serving a life sentence for his role in the 2002 sniper attacks that terrorized the Washington, D.C., area and left 10 people dead, has emerged in recent accounts as a figure caught between two competing narratives. Through a letter he wrote to CNN and the testimony of social worker Carmeta Albarus-Lindo, Malvo is portrayed as a deeply remorseful young man—one who was, in his own framing, a "brainwashed" youth systematically manipulated by the older man he came to see as a surrogate father figure.

## A Portrait of Manipulation

According to Albarus-Lindo, who has spent considerable time studying Malvo's psychological history, the teenager fell under the powerful influence of John Allen Muhammad, the mastermind behind the attacks. Malvo, who was just 17 years old during the killing spree, is described as a vulnerable adolescent who lacked a stable paternal presence in his life. Muhammad, this account suggests, exploited that vulnerability, molding the impressionable young man into an instrument of his deadly campaign.

In his correspondence with CNN, Malvo reportedly expresses genuine contrition for the lives lost and the trauma inflicted upon the region. His words paint a picture of a person who, with the passage of time and physical distance from Muhammad's control, has come to reckon with the enormity of what he participated in. This framing positions Malvo not as a cold-blooded killer acting of his own volition, but as a young person whose moral compass was hijacked by a predatory adult.

## The Prosecution's Firm Rejection

Prosecutors, however, categorically reject this sympathetic characterization. In their view, Malvo—despite his youth at the time—was fully aware of his actions and made deliberate choices to embrace a life of violence and crime. They contend that the "brainwashing" defense minimizes his personal responsibility and offers a convenient excuse for calculated participation in murder. To these officials, Malvo knew exactly what he was doing when he took part in the shootings, and his age does not absolve him of accountability for the terror he helped unleash.

## An Ongoing Debate

The contrasting portrayals underscore a persistent and difficult debate surrounding Malvo's culpability. At its heart lie profound questions about juvenile responsibility, the psychology of coercion, and the extent to which a young person can be held morally and legally accountable for actions committed under another's influence. The disagreement also speaks to the lasting scars left by the sniper rampage—a series of random attacks that gripped an entire region in fear and forever altered the lives of victims' families.

As the years pass, Malvo's case continues to provoke reflection on where justice should draw the line between manipulation and choice, and how society should reckon with those who commit grave crimes in their youth.

# Five Years After Sniper Attacks, Malvo Speaks Out on His Transformation

*By CNN Staff*

Five years after a series of sniper shootings terrorized the Washington, D.C., area and left 10 people dead, convicted sniper Lee Boyd Malvo is offering a rare glimpse into his mind and the man who he says manipulated him into becoming a killer.

In a handwritten letter to CNN, Malvo, now in his early 20s and serving multiple life sentences without the possibility of parole, expressed remorse for his role in the October 2002 shootings that paralyzed communities across the region.

"I was a monster," Malvo wrote. "If you look up the definition, that's what a monster is. I was a ghoul. I was a thief. I stole people's lives."

## A Social Worker's Insight

Carmeta Albarus-Lindo, a social worker who spent extensive time with Malvo while preparing for his defense, has argued that the teenage Malvo was systematically brainwashed by John Allen Muhammad, the older man who became a father figure to the fatherless boy from Jamaica.

According to Albarus-Lindo, Muhammad exploited Malvo's desperate need for a paternal figure, gradually indoctrinating him and stripping away his ability to think independently. She traveled to Jamaica and Antigua to trace Malvo's troubled upbringing, which she says left him vulnerable to Muhammad's influence.

Albarus-Lindo described how Muhammad allegedly used a combination of ideological instruction, isolation, and control to reshape Malvo's identity, transforming a once-promising young man into a willing accomplice in the killings.

She noted that in her later conversations with Malvo, he had come to understand how thoroughly he had been manipulated and expressed genuine remorse for his actions—a stark contrast to the cold demeanor he displayed during the trials.

## Prosecutors Push Back

Prosecutors who worked to convict Malvo have rejected the brainwashing narrative, maintaining that he was a willing and active participant in the shootings.

They point to evidence presented during the trials showing Malvo was often the triggerman, and argue that he demonstrated clear intent and awareness of his actions. To prosecutors, the depiction of Malvo as a helpless victim of manipulation minimizes his responsibility for the lives he took and the terror he inflicted on the community.

They emphasize that regardless of Muhammad's influence, Malvo made choices that resulted in the deaths of innocent people going about their daily lives—pumping gas, shopping, and mowing lawns.

## Victims' Families React

For the families of those killed, the passage of five years has done little to ease their grief, and reactions to Malvo's expressions of remorse remain deeply divided.

Some family members find little comfort in his words, viewing them as too little, too late for the loved ones they lost. Others have expressed a measured willingness to consider that Malvo, who was only 17 at the time of the shootings, may have been a different kind of victim in the tragedy—though this does not diminish their pain.

The shootings left an indelible mark on the region, where residents lived in fear for three weeks in the fall of 2002, uncertain when or where the next shot might come.

## Muhammad's Ex-Wife Weighs In

Mildred Muhammad, John Allen Muhammad's ex-wife, has offered her own perspective on the case. She has long maintained that the entire sniper spree was ultimately connected to her ex-husband's desire to kill her and regain custody of their children, using the random shootings as a smokescreen to disguise his true target.

Her account adds another layer to the complex motivations behind the attacks, suggesting personal vengeance lay at the heart of what appeared to be random violence.

## Two Divergent Paths

While Malvo has been sentenced to life in prison, John Allen Muhammad received a death sentence for his role as the mastermind of the killings.

As the fifth anniversary of the shootings passes, the case continues to raise difficult questions about culpability, manipulation, and the point at which a young person can be held fully responsible for horrific crimes committed under the influence of a controlling adult.

For Malvo, the coming decades in prison offer time to reflect on the lives he took—and, as his letter suggests, on the person he once was and the man he hopes to become.

# Under His Influence: The Question That Haunted the Beltway Sniper Case

*Examining the disturbing relationship between John Allen Muhammad and the teenager who followed him into terror*

---

For three weeks in October 2002, the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area lived in a state of siege. Ten people were killed and three critically injured by sniper fire that came without warning—at gas stations, in parking lots, outside schools. When police finally captured the perpetrators sleeping at a Maryland rest stop, they found not the lone gunman many had imagined, but two people: John Allen Muhammad, 41, and Lee Boyd Malvo, a 17-year-old boy from Jamaica.

The age gap between them would become central to one of the case's most enduring questions: Was Malvo a willing partner in murder, or had Muhammad so thoroughly reshaped the teenager's mind that the boy had effectively surrendered his own will?

## A Father Figure Turned Predator

Malvo's early life was marked by abandonment. His father left when he was young, and his mother, Una James, moved frequently, sometimes leaving her son behind in the care of others. When Malvo met Muhammad in Antigua around 2000, the older man offered what the boy had never known: attention, structure, and the promise of belonging.

"You have to understand what a vulnerable target looks like," said a former juvenile justice social worker who reviewed cases involving adult-youth criminal partnerships. "A child who's been abandoned, who's searching for identity, who has no stable adult—that child will attach to whoever offers consistency. It doesn't matter if that person is dangerous. Sometimes the danger is invisible to them because the attention feels like love."

Muhammad, who had lost custody of his own children in a bitter dispute with his ex-wife, appeared to fill a paternal void. Malvo began calling him "Dad." Witnesses who encountered the pair described Malvo as deferential, almost worshipful, rarely speaking unless Muhammad prompted him.

## The Mechanics of Control

Investigators who worked the case described a relationship that went beyond ordinary influence.

"When we started pulling apart their daily life, it became clear this wasn't two equals planning together," said one former investigator familiar with the interrogations. "Muhammad controlled everything—what the kid ate, when he slept, what he read, how he trained. He'd put him on a strict diet, made him exercise, had him studying materials. It was regimented like boot camp, but with one instructor and one recruit."

According to court testimony and later interviews, Muhammad allegedly restricted Malvo's diet to crackers and honey at times, controlled his access to the outside world, and immersed him in a worldview that mixed racial grievance, apocalyptic thinking, and personal vendetta. Prosecutors would later argue that the ultimate goal of the shooting spree was to create chaos as cover for Muhammad's real aim: killing his ex-wife and regaining his children.

"He isolated that boy from anyone who could offer a competing version of reality," the social worker explained. "That's the textbook foundation. You cut off outside voices, you control the physical body through food and sleep, and you become the only source of meaning. At seventeen, the brain isn't finished developing—especially the parts that handle impulse control and long-term judgment. A skilled manipulator knows how to exploit that."

## The Defense's Central Argument

When Malvo went to trial, his defense attorneys built their case around the concept of indoctrination. They brought in mental health experts who testified that Malvo had been systematically conditioned, that his capacity for independent moral judgment had been compromised by a man he regarded as a god-like authority.

The defense presented Malvo as a boy who had been "captured" psychologically—not held at gunpoint, but bound by something arguably stronger: the desperate loyalty of an abandoned child to the only father he'd ever felt he had.

Prosecutors countered fiercely. Malvo, they noted, was old enough to know that shooting strangers was wrong. He had pulled the trigger. He had, at times, appeared to boast. Brainwashing, they suggested, was a convenient theory to escape accountability.

"There's always tension in these cases between explanation and excuse," the former investigator acknowledged. "Understanding why someone did something isn't the same as saying they bear no responsibility. Both things were true here. That kid was manipulated—I have no doubt. And that kid also killed people. The jury had to sit with both."

## Mildred's Perspective

Perhaps no one understood John Allen Muhammad's capacity for control better than Mildred Muhammad, his ex-wife—the woman investigators say was the intended final target of the entire campaign.

In the years since, Mildred has spoken publicly about the man she once married and the fear that defined the end of their relationship. She has described a husband whose charm could turn to menace, a man capable of methodical planning and psychological domination.

"I knew what he was capable of because I lived it," Mildred has said in her public accounts of the ordeal. "He told me I would never see my children again, and then he disappeared with them. This was a man who could make you doubt your own mind."

Her testimony offered a chilling frame for understanding Malvo. If Muhammad could exert that kind of control over an adult woman who had known him for years, what could he do to a lonely teenage boy who saw him as salvation?

Mildred has expressed a complicated compassion regarding Malvo—recognizing him as another person caught in the orbit of a dangerous man, while never losing sight of the victims and their families. Her advocacy since the case has focused largely on domestic violence awareness, reframing the sniper attacks not as random terror but as an extension of one man's obsessive rage against his family.

"People saw random shootings," she has emphasized in her advocacy work. "I saw a domestic violence case that no one recognized until it was too late."

## What the Science Says

The term "brainwashing" carries dramatic connotations, but psychologists tend to speak more precisely about coercive control, undue influence, and traumatic bonding. These concepts describe real, documented phenomena—the same dynamics seen in cults, abusive relationships, and cases of exploitation.

"We resist the word 'brainwashing' because it sounds like science fiction, like someone flipped a switch," the social worker noted. "The reality is more gradual and, honestly, more disturbing. It happens through relationship. Through need. Through slowly rewriting what a young person believes is normal and necessary. And the younger and more wounded the person, the more effective it is."

Adolescent development research supports the notion that teenagers are more susceptible to peer and authority influence, more prone to risk-taking, and less capable of the long-term consequence assessment that characterizes adult cognition. The U.S. Supreme Court has since cited such research in decisions limiting the harshest sentences for juvenile offenders.

## The Verdicts and the Aftermath

John Allen Muhammad was convicted and sentenced to death. He was executed in Virginia in November 2009, largely unrepentant and silent about his motives to the end.

Malvo received multiple life sentences.
